scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire study (title, objectives, methods, results, and discussion) concerns postacute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC/Long COVID) identified via EHR phenotyping across 58 US hospitals; Lyme disease is not mentioned anywhere in the document's text, tables, or figures.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a peer-reviewed cohort study (JAMA Network Open, 2026) that used a validated AI phenotyping algorithm (P2RC) on electronic health record data from 457,950 COVID-19 patients across 58 hospitals in four US regions (New England, Southeast Texas, Southern California, Western Pennsylvania) to estimate how many people actually develop Long COVID (PASC), compared with how many are captured by standard diagnostic coding. The algorithm identified PASC in 16.28% of COVID-19 patients overall, more than double the under-7% typically found by diagnosis-code-based surveillance, and found that 89.31% of identified PASC cases involved at least one chronic condition requiring ongoing management (14.54% of all COVID-19 patients in the cohort). The study also found substantial regional differences in which organ systems were affected, and found that cumulative PASC prevalence kept rising through mid-2024, suggesting an accumulating rather than resolving burden. The document reports no dollar costs, lost-income, caregiving-time, or out-of-pocket figures; its burden evidence is limited to prevalence, chronicity, and surveillance-gap percentages drawn from EHR/diagnostic-coding data.

contextual_issues: Caregiver burden and informal caregiving time are not mentioned or quantified anywhere in this document.

Direct medical costs, out-of-pocket costs, and indirect costs (lost income, productivity loss) are not quantified by this document; it only cites, without adopting as its own measurement, that PASC patients 'generate approximately 1.5 times higher health care costs than matched controls' from two external studies (refs 37-38), with no dollar figure or price year given.

Elevated PASC-related hospitalization risk (odds ratio 1.28, 95% CI 1.23-1.33) is mentioned only as a citation from an external OpenSAFELY cohort study (ref 5), not as this document's own measured result.

Downstream system consequences of under-ascertainment -- 'health systems cannot accurately project capacity,' 'disability programs cannot fully recognize the true burden,' 'payers cannot develop appropriate reimbursement models,' 'investigators cannot efficiently recruit participants' -- are described narratively but not quantified.

Fragmented, specialty-siloed clinical management of PASC symptoms (fatigue in primary care, dysautonomia in cardiology, new-onset diabetes in endocrinology, cognitive complaints in neurology) is described qualitatively but not assigned any burden metric.

Insurance and access barriers are referenced only indirectly via the stated limitation that patients with 'limited or fragmented health care engagement' may be underrepresented, causing underestimation of PASC prevalence; no quantified access-barrier metric is reported.

External meta-analytic comparator prevalence figures (43% global PASC prevalence; 45% unresolved symptoms at ~4 months; 30% persistent symptoms at 24 months) are cited for context but are not this document's own measured findings and use different case definitions and time windows than its own cumulative 'ever identified' measure.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, direct non-medical cost (travel, paid help), or indirect cost (lost income, productivity, caregiving time) data are reported anywhere in this document; linking this cohort's chronic-PASC case counts to claims or cost data would be required to model dollar burden.

No COVID-19-negative comparator group was included, so excess incidence of chronic conditions attributable to PASC above background population rates cannot be quantified (an explicit limitation stated by the authors).

Site-specific U09.9 diagnostic-code counts were not directly compared to phenotyping-derived counts at the same sites; the surveillance-gap claim relies on previously published U09.9 sensitivity estimates rather than a matched within-study comparison.

EHR chart review validation was performed via distributional robustness testing only, not site-specific manual review, at 3 of the 4 regions, so site-level precision/recall of the phenotyping algorithm remain unquantified.

The national extrapolation of ~15 million individuals applies the pooled 14.54% cohort rate uniformly to an external national case count without regional, demographic, or health-care-access-based reweighting, and would need such adjustment (plus independent validation) to support a more representative national burden estimate.
comparison_boundaries: Do not equate 'cumulative prevalence' (proportion of COVID-19 patients ever identified with PASC through a given quarter) with 'current active case' prevalence; the document explicitly states resolution cannot be reliably determined from retrospective EHR data, so cumulative prevalence should be read as an 'ever identified' measure, not a current-caseload estimate.

Do not pool the four regional PASC prevalence estimates as equivalent-confidence inputs to one range: the regions differ by up to 50-fold in sample size (5,002 COVID-19 cases in Southeast Texas vs. 252,649 in Western Pennsylvania), and Southeast Texas's small sample produced an unstable quarterly incidence estimate (60.78%, 95% CI 46.11%-74.16%, Q1 2024) and a nonsignificant temporal trend (P=.07) -- these are not comparable-precision measurements of one underlying rate.

Do not pool the ~15 million national extrapolation with the cohort's own regional/aggregate rates; the national figure combines this study's pooled 14.54% rate with an external national case count (CDC surveillance, ref 36) under different population coverage and data-collection assumptions, and the authors themselves flag it as requiring cautious interpretation.

spec.title: Long COVID Phenotyping vs. Diagnosis-Code Surveillance Gap Explorer
spec.boundary: This simulator reflects only what a 2026 JAMA Network Open EHR cohort study (457,950 COVID-19 patients, 58 hospitals, 4 US regions, Q2 2020-Q2 2024) reported: AI phenotyping-identified PASC (Long COVID) prevalence, chronic-condition prevalence, a cited diagnosis-code surveillance benchmark, and the study's own cautious national and decade-ahead projections. It contains no dollar costs, income loss, or caregiving-time data, because the source document reports none; all cost language is intentionally absent.

takeaway.patient: This study used AI analysis of electronic health records across four US regions to look for Long COVID symptoms, and found it in about 16% of COVID-19 patients overall (ranging 13.64%-22.69% by region) - more than double what standard diagnosis coding typically captures (under 7%). Of those identified, the study found about 89% went on to have at least one ongoing chronic condition, not a short-term illness, and the share of people found to have Long COVID kept rising through mid-2024 rather than leveling off. The study found that PASC patients were more likely to be female and older than the overall COVID-19 population. This was measured in four specific US regions using hospital health-record data, not a nationally representative sample.
takeaway.care: Phenotyping algorithms applied to this four-region EHR cohort identified PASC in roughly double the share of COVID-19 patients that standard diagnosis coding typically captures, and found that about 89% of identified cases involved an ongoing chronic condition (14.54% of all COVID-19 patients in the cohort). The study also found that organ-system involvement differed significantly by region and that cumulative prevalence kept accumulating rather than resolving through mid-2024 in three of the four regions (Southeast Texas's upward trend did not reach statistical significance, likely reflecting its much smaller sample). The authors describe current specialty-siloed coding (fatigue in primary care, dysautonomia in cardiology, new-onset diabetes in endocrinology, cognitive complaints in neurology) as leaving most managed PASC cases invisible to population-level surveillance.
takeaway.policy: This cohort study found a large gap between AI-phenotyping-identified PASC prevalence (16.28% overall, 13.64%-22.69% regionally) and the diagnosis-code-based surveillance benchmark it cites (under 7%, drawn from external studies), with 14.54% of all COVID-19 patients in the cohort developing a chronic condition. The authors' own national extrapolation - applying this cohort's 14.54% chronic-PASC rate to roughly 103 million cited US COVID-19 cases - suggests on the order of 15 million affected individuals, but they explicitly caution this estimate 'should be interpreted cautiously' given regional and demographic coverage limits. A separately projected 13%-81% decade-compounded increase applies only to the three regions whose quarterly trend reached statistical significance.

patient: Patients or caregivers dealing with lingering post-COVID symptoms without a formal diagnosis on their chart may find it useful to understand, from this study, that diagnosis coding is reported to miss most Long COVID cases - this could be a plain-language question to raise with a clinician, not something to resolve alone.

Because the study found most identified cases involved an ongoing chronic condition rather than a short illness, patients and caregivers may want to factor ongoing rather than one-time specialist follow-up into their own planning conversations.

Patient advocacy groups could cite this study's finding that cumulative identification kept rising rather than leveling off through mid-2024 to support continued attention to long-term post-COVID care needs.
care: Use the regional chronic-PASC prevalence range (12.03%-19.88%) and the accumulating (not resolving) trend in three of four regions to scenario-plan ongoing specialty referral capacity, while treating the Southeast Texas estimate as less certain given its smaller sample and non-significant trend.

The finding that PASC symptoms are managed under fragmented specialty-specific codes without a coordinating link back to antecedent COVID-19 infection may be worth checking against your own site's coding and referral workflow.

Consider whether local tracking distinguishes 'ever identified' cumulative PASC prevalence from current active caseload, since the study notes retrospective EHR data cannot reliably determine symptom resolution.
policy: Use the gap between phenotyping-identified prevalence (13.64%-22.69% regionally) and the cited diagnosis-code-based surveillance benchmark (under 7%) to inform discussions about whether disability-recognition and reimbursement systems calibrated to diagnosis-code counts may be structurally underrecognizing chronic PASC burden.

Treat the study's own ~15 million national projection and 13%-81% decade-compounded increase range as illustrative, authors'-own-cautioned projections requiring independent validation and demographic reweighting before use in funding or capacity decisions, not as validated national counts.

Consider supporting a matched, within-system comparison of phenotyping-derived versus diagnosis-code-based case counts at the same sites, since this study's surveillance-gap benchmark comes from externally cited studies rather than a direct comparison in this cohort.

## Data and parameters
All figures come from a JAMA Network Open (2026) EHR-based cohort study of 457,950 COVID-19 patients across 58 hospitals in four US regions (New England, Southeast Texas, Southern California, Western Pennsylvania), using a validated AI phenotyping algorithm (P2RC) to identify PASC (Long COVID), Q2 2020-Q2 2024.

- Phenotyping-identified PASC prevalence (16.28% overall; 13.64%-22.69% regionally) and chronic PASC prevalence (14.54% overall; 12.03%-19.88% regionally) are the study's own observed measurements (Table 1, Table 2).
- The code-based surveillance comparator (under 7% broadly; a separately cited 4.9%-19.0% U09.9 sensitivity range) comes from external studies (refs 15-17, 35) adopted by the document as its benchmark, not from a matched within-study comparison at the same sites.
- The ~103 million national COVID-19 case count is an external citation (CDC surveillance, ref 36); the national chronic-PASC estimate combining it with this cohort's 14.54% rate is the document's own projection, which the authors state should be interpreted cautiously.
- The 13%-81% decade-compounded increase range reflects the document's own extrapolation from quarterly incidence-rate-ratio trends that reached statistical significance in 3 of 4 regions (New England, Southern California, Western Pennsylvania); Southeast Texas's trend did not reach significance (P=.07) and is excluded from that range.

## Limitations
The surveillance-gap comparator relies on claims/ICD-10-coded diagnosis data (U09.9 and related codes); the document itself notes this coding captures a minority of true cases, so any diagnosis-code-based figure referenced here likely undercounts actual PASC burden.

The pooled 14.54% chronic-PASC rate used in the national projection has not been broken down by sex, age, or race/ethnicity in this document, even though the cohort itself found PASC patients skewed older, more comorbid, and more female (60.0%-66.0% female across regions, versus 60.07% female in the overall COVID-19 cohort). Federal survey data sources such as NHIS and BRFSS generally support disaggregated analysis by these characteristics even though this document did not perform one.

The document also describes a systemic evidence gap: current ICD-10-CM coding practice provides no pathway linking specialty-specific diagnoses (e.g., fatigue in primary care, dysautonomia in cardiology, new-onset diabetes in endocrinology, cognitive complaints in neurology) back to antecedent COVID-19 infection, leaving most managed PASC cases invisible to population-level surveillance even while actively treated in clinical care.

No dollar costs, income-loss, or caregiving-time figures are reported anywhere in this document; every output here is a prevalence, chronicity, or surveillance-gap percentage or count, not a cost estimate.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- Phenotyping-identified cumulative PASC prevalence among COVID-19 patients (overall, 4-region cohort) (2020-2024): the document reports 16.28% as the share of adults who ever had COVID-19 that ever experienced Long COVID; the national survey's 27 wave(s) in that period ranged from 25.6% to 35.1% (interval bounds 24.9% to 36%), so the document's figure is below every survey wave interval in that period. The survey is self-reported adults; a different definition or population in the document makes a gap expected, so treat it as a prompt to check. The survey has no data for 2020, 2021. Federal source: household survey (self-report), 2022-2024; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Chronic PASC prevalence among all COVID-19 patients in the cohort (2020-2024): the document reports 14.54% as the share of adults who ever had COVID-19 that ever experienced Long COVID; the national survey's 27 wave(s) in that period ranged from 25.6% to 35.1% (interval bounds 24.9% to 36%), so the document's figure is below every survey wave interval in that period. The survey is self-reported adults; a different definition or population in the document makes a gap expected, so treat it as a prompt to check. The survey has no data for 2020, 2021. Federal source: household survey (self-report), 2022-2024; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.

spec.title: Long COVID Phenotyping vs. Diagnosis-Code Surveillance Gap Explorer
spec.boundary: This simulator reflects only what a 2026 JAMA Network Open EHR cohort study (457,950 COVID-19 patients, 58 hospitals, 4 US regions, Q2 2020-Q2 2024) reported: AI phenotyping-identified PASC (Long COVID) prevalence, chronic-condition prevalence, a cited diagnosis-code surveillance benchmark, and the study's own cautious national and decade-ahead projections. It contains no dollar costs, income loss, or caregiving-time data, because the source document reports none; all cost language is intentionally absent.

takeaway.patient: This study used AI analysis of electronic health records across four US regions to look for Long COVID symptoms, and found it in about 16% of COVID-19 patients overall (ranging 13.64%-22.69% by region) - more than double what standard diagnosis coding typically captures (under 7%). Of those identified, the study found about 89% went on to have at least one ongoing chronic condition, not a short-term illness, and the share of people found to have Long COVID kept rising through mid-2024 rather than leveling off. The study found that PASC patients were more likely to be female and older than the overall COVID-19 population. This was measured in four specific US regions using hospital health-record data, not a nationally representative sample.
takeaway.care: Phenotyping algorithms applied to this four-region EHR cohort identified PASC in roughly double the share of COVID-19 patients that standard diagnosis coding typically captures, and found that about 89% of identified cases involved an ongoing chronic condition (14.54% of all COVID-19 patients in the cohort). The study also found that organ-system involvement differed significantly by region and that cumulative prevalence kept accumulating rather than resolving through mid-2024 in three of the four regions (Southeast Texas's upward trend did not reach statistical significance, likely reflecting its much smaller sample). The authors describe current specialty-siloed coding (fatigue in primary care, dysautonomia in cardiology, new-onset diabetes in endocrinology, cognitive complaints in neurology) as leaving most managed PASC cases invisible to population-level surveillance.
takeaway.policy: This cohort study found a large gap between AI-phenotyping-identified PASC prevalence (16.28% overall, 13.64%-22.69% regionally) and the diagnosis-code-based surveillance benchmark it cites (under 7%, drawn from external studies), with 14.54% of all COVID-19 patients in the cohort developing a chronic condition. The authors' own national extrapolation - applying this cohort's 14.54% chronic-PASC rate to roughly 103 million cited US COVID-19 cases - suggests on the order of 15 million affected individuals, but they explicitly caution this estimate 'should be interpreted cautiously' given regional and demographic coverage limits. A separately projected 13%-81% decade-compounded increase applies only to the three regions whose quarterly trend reached statistical significance.

patient: Patients or caregivers dealing with lingering post-COVID symptoms without a formal diagnosis on their chart may find it useful to understand, from this study, that diagnosis coding is reported to miss most Long COVID cases - this could be a plain-language question to raise with a clinician, not something to resolve alone.

Because the study found most identified cases involved an ongoing chronic condition rather than a short illness, patients and caregivers may want to factor ongoing rather than one-time specialist follow-up into their own planning conversations.

Patient advocacy groups could cite this study's finding that cumulative identification kept rising rather than leveling off through mid-2024 to support continued attention to long-term post-COVID care needs.
care: Use the regional chronic-PASC prevalence range (12.03%-19.88%) and the accumulating (not resolving) trend in three of four regions to scenario-plan ongoing specialty referral capacity, while treating the Southeast Texas estimate as less certain given its smaller sample and non-significant trend.

The finding that PASC symptoms are managed under fragmented specialty-specific codes without a coordinating link back to antecedent COVID-19 infection may be worth checking against your own site's coding and referral workflow.

Consider whether local tracking distinguishes 'ever identified' cumulative PASC prevalence from current active caseload, since the study notes retrospective EHR data cannot reliably determine symptom resolution.
policy: Use the gap between phenotyping-identified prevalence (13.64%-22.69% regionally) and the cited diagnosis-code-based surveillance benchmark (under 7%) to inform discussions about whether disability-recognition and reimbursement systems calibrated to diagnosis-code counts may be structurally underrecognizing chronic PASC burden.

Treat the study's own ~15 million national projection and 13%-81% decade-compounded increase range as illustrative, authors'-own-cautioned projections requiring independent validation and demographic reweighting before use in funding or capacity decisions, not as validated national counts.

Consider supporting a matched, within-system comparison of phenotyping-derived versus diagnosis-code-based case counts at the same sites, since this study's surveillance-gap benchmark comes from externally cited studies rather than a direct comparison in this cohort.
